messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 68
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: Widowed
- Occupation: Dancer
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening motor vehicle collision
- Pcl5: 67

The first time he talked about the accident, Solomon’s hands began to move—not the swift, controlled gestures of a dancer, but a slow, tremulous tracing of air, as if he were trying to catch something just out of reach. He was sixty-eight, a widower of three years, and had been a professional dancer for most of his life. He came to my office at the urging of his daughter, who had noticed he no longer left the apartment except to buy food, and even then only after dark. He sat on the edge of the chair, spine straight, feet planted, as though waiting for a cue that never arrived.

The collision happened on a Tuesday afternoon, three months ago, on a rain-slicked highway outside the city. Solomon had been driving home from a rehearsal—a solo piece he had been choreographing for a small contemporary company. He remembers the light fading, the wipers struggling, the sudden glare of headlights from a pickup truck that had crossed the median. He remembers the sound: a long, metallic tear, then silence. He woke in the hospital with three broken ribs, a fractured clavicle, and a deep gash along his right thigh that required forty stitches. The driver of the other vehicle died at the scene.

Physically, Solomon healed. The ribs mended; the clavicle knit; the thigh scarred over into a thick, puckered line. But something else did not. He stopped dancing. Not because his body refused—the choreographer had offered him a rest period, but Solomon knew he could have returned within weeks. Instead, he told the company manager he was retiring. He said it quietly, without emotion, as though reading a weather report. Then he hung up and sat in his living room for the rest of the day, watching the shadows crawl across the floor.

Now, in session, Solomon describes a world that has become thin and treacherous. He no longer drives. He flinches at the sound of rain on the window, at the rumble of a truck passing his building. Once, a car backfired outside the grocery store, and he dropped to his knees on the pavement, heart tearing, unable to breathe for nearly a minute. His daughter found him there. He told her it was nothing—just a dizzy spell—but he knew it was the sound, that same tearing sound, playing again inside his skull.

He has nightmares almost every night. In the most recurrent one, he is onstage, spotlit, in the middle of a solo. The music swells, but then the floor begins to dissolve, and he falls through the black, falling and falling, into the headlights of an oncoming truck. He wakes gasping, his hands gripping the sheets, his thighs trembling. He does not tell his daughter. He does not tell anyone. He lies still in the dark, counting his breaths, waiting for the dawn.

The dance studio, once his sanctuary, has become a place of dread. He has not stepped inside it since before the accident. When I ask why, Solomon’s jaw tightens. “It’s gone,” he says. “The feeling—the way my body used to know what to do. I can’t feel it anymore.” He describes a peculiar numbness, a disconnection from his own limbs. He will look at his hands and see them as objects, not as part of himself. Sometimes, while walking to the corner store, he feels a sudden surge of rage—hot, wordless—and he has to stop and clench his fists until it passes. He does not understand where it comes from. He only knows that the world, once full of rhythm and intention, now feels random and menacing.

At home, Solomon avoids the television. He avoids news reports. He avoids the sound of rain. He keeps the blinds shut. He eats standing up, quickly, as if someone might take the plate away. He has not called his old dancers, or accepted any dinner invitations. The loneliness is vast, but it is also a kind of protection—a small, dark room where nothing can surprise him. When I ask him what he hopes for, he looks at me with tired eyes. “I just want the noise to stop,” he says. “Inside my head. I want to stop remembering.”
